requirements.section: Routing HTTP Messages > Message Forwarding > Max-Forwards
requirements.text: If the received value is zero (0), the intermediary MUST NOT forward the request; instead, the intermediary MUST respond as the final recipient.

requirements.section: Routing HTTP Messages > Message Forwarding > Max-Forwards
requirements.text: If the received Max-Forwards value is greater than zero, the intermediary MUST generate an updated Max-Forwards field in the forwarded message with a field value that is the lesser of a) the received value decremented by one (1) or b) the recipient's maximum supported value for Max-Forwards.

requirements.section: Routing HTTP Messages > Message Forwarding > Via
requirements.text: However, comments in Via are optional, and a recipient MAY remove them prior to forwarding the message.

requirements.section: Routing HTTP Messages > Message Forwarding > Via
requirements.text: However, if the real host is considered to be sensitive information, a sender MAY replace it with a pseudonym.

requirements.section: Routing HTTP Messages > Message Forwarding > Via
requirements.text: An intermediary MAY combine an ordered subsequence of Via header field list members into a single member if the entries have identical received-protocol values.

requirements.section: Routing HTTP Messages > Message Forwarding > Via
requirements.text: If a port is not provided, a recipient MAY interpret that as meaning it was received on the default port, if any, for the received-protocol.

requirements.section: Routing HTTP Messages > Message Forwarding > Via
requirements.text: A sender MAY generate comments to identify the software of each recipient, analogous to the User-Agent and Server header fields.

requirements.section: Routing HTTP Messages > Message Forwarding > Via
requirements.text: An HTTP-to-HTTP gateway MUST send an appropriate Via header field in each inbound request message and MAY send a Via header field in forwarded response messages.

requirements.section: Routing HTTP Messages > Message Forwarding > Via
requirements.text: A sender MUST NOT combine members that have different received-protocol values.

requirements.section: Routing HTTP Messages > Message Forwarding > Via
requirements.text: A proxy MUST send an appropriate Via header field, as described below, in each message that it forwards.

requirements.section: Routing HTTP Messages > Message Forwarding > Via
requirements.text: If not enabled, such an intermediary SHOULD replace each received-by host of any host behind the firewall by an appropriate pseudonym for that host.

requirements.section: Routing HTTP Messages > Message Forwarding > Via
requirements.text: An intermediary used as a portal through a network firewall SHOULD NOT forward the names and ports of hosts within the firewall region unless it is explicitly enabled to do so.

requirements.section: Routing HTTP Messages > Message Forwarding > Via
requirements.text: A sender SHOULD NOT combine multiple list members unless they are all under the same organizational control and the hosts have already been replaced by pseudonyms.

requirements.section: Routing HTTP Messages > Message Forwarding
requirements.text: An intermediary not acting as a tunnel MUST implement the Connection header field, as specified in Section 7.6.1, and exclude fields from being forwarded that are only intended for the incoming connection.

requirements.section: Routing HTTP Messages > Message Forwarding
requirements.text: An intermediary MUST NOT forward a message to itself unless it is protected from an infinite request loop.

requirements.section: Routing HTTP Messages > Message Transformations
requirements.text: If a proxy receives a target URI with a host name that is not a fully qualified domain name, it MAY add its own domain to the host name it received when forwarding the request.

requirements.section: Routing HTTP Messages > Message Transformations
requirements.text: A proxy MAY transform the content of a message that does not contain a no-transform cache directive.

requirements.section: Routing HTTP Messages > Message Transformations
requirements.text: A proxy MUST NOT change the host name if the target URI contains a fully qualified domain name.

requirements.section: Routing HTTP Messages > Message Transformations
requirements.text: A proxy MUST NOT modify the "absolute-path" and "query" parts of the received target URI when forwarding it to the next inbound server except as required by that forwarding protocol.

requirements.section: Routing HTTP Messages > Message Transformations
requirements.text: A proxy MUST NOT transform the content (Section 6.4) of a response message that contains a no-transform cache directive (Section 5.2.2.6 of [CACHING]).

requirements.section: Routing HTTP Messages > Message Transformations
requirements.text: A proxy SHOULD NOT modify header fields that provide information about the endpoints of the communication chain, the resource state, or the selected representation (other than the content) unless the field's definition specifically allows such modification or the modification is deemed necessary for privacy or security.

requirements.section: Routing HTTP Messages > Upgrade
requirements.text: A client MAY send a list of protocol names in the Upgrade header field of a request to invite the server to switch to one or more of the named protocols, in order of descending preference, before sending the final response.

requirements.section: Routing HTTP Messages > Upgrade
requirements.text: A server MAY choose to ignore the order of preference indicated by the client and select the new protocol(s) based on other factors, such as the nature of the request or the current load on the server.

requirements.section: Routing HTTP Messages > Upgrade
requirements.text: A server MAY ignore a received Upgrade header field if it wishes to continue using the current protocol on that connection.

requirements.section: Routing HTTP Messages > Upgrade
requirements.text: A server MAY send an Upgrade header field in any other response to advertise that it implements support for upgrading to the listed protocols, in order of descending preference, when appropriate for a future request.

requirements.section: Routing HTTP Messages > Upgrade
requirements.text: A server MUST NOT switch to a protocol that was not indicated by the client in the corresponding request's Upgrade header field.

requirements.section: Routing HTTP Messages > Upgrade
requirements.text: A server MUST NOT switch protocols unless the received message semantics can be honored by the new protocol; an OPTIONS request can be honored by any protocol.

requirements.section: Routing HTTP Messages > Upgrade
requirements.text: A sender of Upgrade MUST also send an "Upgrade" connection option in the Connection header field (Section 7.6.1) to inform intermediaries not to forward this field.

requirements.section: Routing HTTP Messages > Upgrade
requirements.text: If a server receives both an Upgrade and an Expect header field with the "100-continue" expectation (Section 10.1.1), the server MUST send a 100 (Continue) response before sending a 101 (Switching Protocols) response.

requirements.section: Routing HTTP Messages > Upgrade
requirements.text: A server that receives an Upgrade header field in an HTTP/1.0 request MUST ignore that Upgrade field.

requirements.section: Routing HTTP Messages > Upgrade
requirements.text: A server that sends a 101 (Switching Protocols) response MUST send an Upgrade header field to indicate the new protocol(s) to which the connection is being switched; if multiple protocol layers are being switched, the sender MUST list the protocols in layer-ascending order.

requirements.section: Routing HTTP Messages > Upgrade
requirements.text: A server that sends a 426 (Upgrade Required) response MUST send an Upgrade header field to indicate the acceptable protocols, in order of descending preference.

requirements.section: Routing HTTP Messages > Upgrade
requirements.text: Although protocol names are registered with a preferred case, recipients SHOULD use case-insensitive comparison when matching each protocol-name to supported protocols.

requirements.section: Representation Data and Metadata > Content-Type > Media Type
requirements.text: The type/subtype MAY be followed by semicolon-delimited parameters (Section 5.6.6) in the form of name/value pairs.

requirements.section: Representation Data and Metadata > Content-Type > Multipart Types
requirements.text: The message body is itself a protocol element; a sender MUST generate only CRLF to represent line breaks between body parts.

requirements.section: Representation Data and Metadata > Content-Type
requirements.text: If a Content-Type header field is not present, the recipient MAY either assume a media type of "application/octet-stream" ([RFC2046], Section 4.5.1) or examine the data to determine its type.

requirements.section: Representation Data and Metadata > Content-Type
requirements.text: A sender that generates a message containing content SHOULD generate a Content-Type header field in that message unless the intended media type of the enclosed representation is unknown to the sender.

requirements.section: Representation Data and Metadata > Content-Encoding > Content Codings > Compress Coding
requirements.text: A recipient SHOULD consider "x-compress" to be equivalent to "compress".

requirements.section: Representation Data and Metadata > Content-Encoding > Content Codings > Gzip Coding
requirements.text: A recipient SHOULD consider "x-gzip" to be equivalent to "gzip".

requirements.section: Representation Data and Metadata > Content-Encoding
requirements.text: An origin server MAY respond with a status code of 415 (Unsupported Media Type) if a representation in the request message has a content coding that is not acceptable.

requirements.section: Representation Data and Metadata > Content-Encoding
requirements.text: If one or more encodings have been applied to a representation, the sender that applied the encodings MUST generate a Content-Encoding header field that lists the content codings in the order in which they were applied.

requirements.section: Representation Data and Metadata > Content-Encoding
requirements.text: Note that the coding named "identity" is reserved for its special role in Accept-Encoding and thus SHOULD NOT be included.

requirements.section: Representation Data and Metadata > Content-Language
requirements.text: Content-Language MAY be applied to any media type -- it is not limited to textual documents.

requirements.section: Representation Data and Metadata > Content-Language
requirements.text: Multiple languages MAY be listed for content that is intended for multiple audiences.

requirements.section: Representation Data and Metadata > Content-Length
requirements.text: Likewise, a sender MUST NOT forward a message with a Content-Length header field value that does not match the ABNF above, with one exception: a recipient of a Content-Length header field value consisting of the same decimal value repeated as a comma-separated list (e.g, "Content-Length: 42, 42") MAY either reject the message as invalid or replace that invalid field value with a single instance of the decimal value, since this likely indicates that a duplicate was generated or combined by an upstream message processor.

requirements.section: Representation Data and Metadata > Content-Length
requirements.text: As a result, a sender MUST NOT forward a message with a Content-Length header field value that is known to be incorrect.

requirements.section: Representation Data and Metadata > Content-Length
requirements.text: A server MAY send a Content-Length header field in a response to a HEAD request (Section 9.3.2); a server MUST NOT send Content-Length in such a response unless its field value equals the decimal number of octets that would have been sent in the content of a response if the same request had used the GET method.

requirements.section: Representation Data and Metadata > Content-Length
requirements.text: A server MAY send a Content-Length header field in a 304 (Not Modified) response to a conditional GET request (Section 15.4.5); a server MUST NOT send Content-Length in such a response unless its field value equals the decimal number of octets that would have been sent in the content of a 200 (OK) response to the same request.

requirements.section: Representation Data and Metadata > Content-Length
requirements.text: A server MUST NOT send a Content-Length header field in any response with a status code of 1xx (Informational) or 204 (No Content).

requirements.section: Representation Data and Metadata > Content-Length
requirements.text: A server MUST NOT send a Content-Length header field in any 2xx (Successful) response to a CONNECT request (Section 9.3.6).

requirements.section: Representation Data and Metadata > Content-Length
requirements.text: Since there is no predefined limit to the length of content, a recipient MUST anticipate potentially large decimal numerals and prevent parsing errors due to integer conversion overflows or precision loss due to integer conversion (Section 17.5).

requirements.section: Representation Data and Metadata > Content-Length
requirements.text: Aside from the cases defined above, in the absence of Transfer-Encoding, an origin server SHOULD send a Content-Length header field when the content size is known prior to sending the complete header section.

requirements.section: Representation Data and Metadata > Content-Length
requirements.text: A user agent SHOULD NOT send a Content-Length header field when the request message does not contain content and the method semantics do not anticipate such data.

requirements.section: Representation Data and Metadata > Content-Length
requirements.text: A user agent SHOULD send Content-Length in a request when the method defines a meaning for enclosed content and it is not sending Transfer-Encoding.

requirements.section: Representation Data and Metadata > Content-Location
requirements.text: If Content-Location is included in a 2xx (Successful) response message and its value refers (after conversion to absolute form) to a URI that is the same as the target URI, then the recipient MAY consider the content to be a current representation of that resource at the time indicated by the message origination date.

requirements.section: Representation Data and Metadata > Content-Location
requirements.text: An origin server MAY use that context to guide in processing the request or to save it for other uses, such as within source links or versioning metadata.

requirements.section: Representation Data and Metadata > Content-Location
requirements.text: However, an origin server MUST NOT use such context information to alter the request semantics.

requirements.section: Representation Data and Metadata > Content-Location
requirements.text: An origin server that receives a Content-Location field in a request message MUST treat the information as transitory request context rather than as metadata to be saved verbatim as part of the representation.

requirements.section: Representation Data and Metadata > Validator Fields > Weak versus Strong
requirements.text: An origin server SHOULD change a weak entity tag whenever it considers prior representations to be unacceptable as a substitute for the current representation.

requirements.section: Representation Data and Metadata > Validator Fields > Last-Modified > Generation
requirements.text: If the last modification time is derived from implementation-specific metadata that evaluates to some time in the future, according to the origin server's clock, then the origin server MUST replace that value with the message origination date.

requirements.section: Representation Data and Metadata > Validator Fields > Last-Modified > Generation
requirements.text: An origin server with a clock (as defined in Section 5.6.7) MUST NOT generate a Last-Modified date that is later than the server's time of message origination (Date, Section 6.6.1).

requirements.section: Representation Data and Metadata > Validator Fields > Last-Modified > Generation
requirements.text: An origin server without a clock MUST NOT generate a Last-Modified date for a response unless that date value was assigned to the resource by some other system (presumably one with a clock).

requirements.section: Representation Data and Metadata > Validator Fields > Last-Modified > Generation
requirements.text: An origin server SHOULD obtain the Last-Modified value of the representation as close as possible to the time that it generates the Date field value for its response.

requirements.section: Representation Data and Metadata > Validator Fields > Last-Modified > Generation
requirements.text: An origin server SHOULD send Last-Modified for any selected representation for which a last modification date can be reasonably and consistently determined, since its use in conditional requests and evaluating cache freshness ([CACHING]) can substantially reduce unnecessary transfers and significantly improve service availability and scalability.

requirements.section: Representation Data and Metadata > Validator Fields > ETag > Generation
requirements.text: An origin server SHOULD send an ETag for any selected representation for which detection of changes can be reasonably and consistently determined, since the entity tag's use in conditional requests and evaluating cache freshness ([CACHING]) can substantially reduce unnecessary transfers and significantly improve service availability, scalability, and reliability.

requirements.section: Representation Data and Metadata > Validator Fields > ETag
requirements.text: A sender MAY send the ETag field in a trailer section (see Section 6.5).

requirements.section: Representation Data and Metadata > Validator Fields > ETag
requirements.text: If an origin server provides an entity tag for a representation and the generation of that entity tag does not satisfy all of the characteristics of a strong validator (Section 8.8.1), then the origin server MUST mark the entity tag as weak by prefixing its opaque value with "W/" (case-sensitive).

requirements.section: Methods > Overview
requirements.text: All general-purpose servers MUST support the methods GET and HEAD.

requirements.section: Methods > Overview
requirements.text: All other methods are OPTIONAL.

requirements.section: Methods > Overview
requirements.text: An origin server that receives a request method that is recognized and implemented, but not allowed for the target resource, SHOULD respond with the 405 (Method Not Allowed) status code.

requirements.section: Methods > Overview
requirements.text: An origin server that receives a request method that is unrecognized or not implemented SHOULD respond with the 501 (Not Implemented) status code.

requirements.section: Methods > Common Method Properties > Safe Methods
requirements.text: If the purpose of such a resource is to perform an unsafe action, then the resource owner MUST disable or disallow that action when it is accessed using a safe request method.

requirements.section: Methods > Common Method Properties > Safe Methods
requirements.text: A user agent SHOULD distinguish between safe and unsafe methods when presenting potential actions to a user, such that the user can be made aware of an unsafe action before it is requested.

requirements.section: Methods > Common Method Properties > Idempotent Methods
requirements.text: A proxy MUST NOT automatically retry non-idempotent requests.

requirements.section: Methods > Common Method Properties > Idempotent Methods
requirements.text: A client SHOULD NOT automatically retry a failed automatic retry.

requirements.section: Methods > Common Method Properties > Idempotent Methods
requirements.text: A client SHOULD NOT automatically retry a request with a non-idempotent method unless it has some means to know that the request semantics are actually idempotent, regardless of the method, or some means to detect that the original request was never applied.

requirements.section: Methods > Method Definitions > GET
requirements.text: The response to a GET request is cacheable; a cache MAY use it to satisfy subsequent GET and HEAD requests unless otherwise indicated by the Cache-Control header field (Section 5.2 of [CACHING]).

requirements.section: Methods > Method Definitions > GET
requirements.text: A client SHOULD NOT generate content in a GET request unless it is made directly to an origin server that has previously indicated, in or out of band, that such a request has a purpose and will be adequately supported.

requirements.section: Methods > Method Definitions > GET
requirements.text: An origin server SHOULD NOT rely on private agreements to receive content, since participants in HTTP communication are often unaware of intermediaries along the request chain.

requirements.section: Methods > Method Definitions > HEAD
requirements.text: However, a server MAY omit header fields for which a value is determined only while generating the content.

requirements.section: Methods > Method Definitions > HEAD
requirements.text: The response to a HEAD request is cacheable; a cache MAY use it to satisfy subsequent HEAD requests unless otherwise indicated by the Cache-Control header field (Section 5.2 of [CACHING]).

requirements.section: Methods > Method Definitions > HEAD
requirements.text: The HEAD method is identical to GET except that the server MUST NOT send content in the response.

requirements.section: Methods > Method Definitions > HEAD
requirements.text: A client SHOULD NOT generate content in a HEAD request unless it is made directly to an origin server that has previously indicated, in or out of band, that such a request has a purpose and will be adequately supported.

requirements.section: Methods > Method Definitions > HEAD
requirements.text: An origin server SHOULD NOT rely on private agreements to receive content, since participants in HTTP communication are often unaware of intermediaries along the request chain.

requirements.section: Methods > Method Definitions > HEAD
requirements.text: The server SHOULD send the same header fields in response to a HEAD request as it would have sent if the request method had been GET.

requirements.section: Methods > Method Definitions > POST
requirements.text: If the result of processing a POST would be equivalent to a representation of an existing resource, an origin server MAY redirect the user agent to that resource by sending a 303 (See Other) response with the existing resource's identifier in the Location field.

requirements.section: Methods > Method Definitions > POST
requirements.text: If one or more resources has been created on the origin server as a result of successfully processing a POST request, the origin server SHOULD send a 201 (Created) response containing a Location header field that provides an identifier for the primary resource created (Section 10.2.2) and a representation that describes the status of the request while referring to the new resource(s).

requirements.section: Methods > Method Definitions > PUT
requirements.text: An origin server MUST NOT send a validator field (Section 8.8), such as an ETag or Last-Modified field, in a successful response to PUT unless the request's representation data was saved without any transformation applied to the content (i.e., the resource's new representation data is identical to the content received in the PUT request) and the validator field value reflects the new representation.

requirements.section: Methods > Method Definitions > PUT
requirements.text: If the origin server will not make the requested PUT state change to the target resource and instead wishes to have it applied to a different resource, such as when the resource has been moved to a different URI, then the origin server MUST send an appropriate 3xx (Redirection) response; the user agent MAY then make its own decision regarding whether or not to redirect the request.

requirements.section: Methods > Method Definitions > PUT
requirements.text: If the target resource does have a current representation and that representation is successfully modified in accordance with the state of the enclosed representation, then the origin server MUST send either a 200 (OK) or a 204 (No Content) response to indicate successful completion of the request.

requirements.section: Methods > Method Definitions > PUT
requirements.text: If the target resource does not have a current representation and the PUT successfully creates one, then the origin server MUST inform the user agent by sending a 201 (Created) response.

requirements.section: Methods > Method Definitions > PUT
requirements.text: An origin server SHOULD verify that the PUT representation is consistent with its configured constraints for the target resource.

requirements.section: Methods > Method Definitions > PUT
requirements.text: When a PUT representation is inconsistent with the target resource, the origin server SHOULD either make them consistent, by transforming the representation or changing the resource configuration, or respond with an appropriate error message containing sufficient information to explain why the representation is unsuitable.

requirements.section: Methods > Method Definitions > PUT
requirements.text: As a result, an origin server SHOULD ignore unrecognized header and trailer fields received in a PUT request (i.e., not save them as part of the resource state).

requirements.section: Methods > Method Definitions > PUT
requirements.text: A service that selects a proper URI on behalf of the client, after receiving a state-changing request, SHOULD be implemented using the POST method rather than PUT.

requirements.section: Methods > Method Definitions > DELETE
requirements.text: If a DELETE method is successfully applied, the origin server SHOULD send

requirements.section: Methods > Method Definitions > DELETE
requirements.text: A client SHOULD NOT generate content in a DELETE request unless it is made directly to an origin server that has previously indicated, in or out of band, that such a request has a purpose and will be adequately supported.

requirements.section: Methods > Method Definitions > DELETE
requirements.text: An origin server SHOULD NOT rely on private agreements to receive content, since participants in HTTP communication are often unaware of intermediaries along the request chain.

requirements.section: Methods > Method Definitions > CONNECT
requirements.text: An origin server MAY accept a CONNECT request, but most origin servers do not implement CONNECT.

requirements.section: Methods > Method Definitions > CONNECT
requirements.text: A client MUST ignore any Content-Length or Transfer-Encoding header fields received in a successful response to CONNECT.

requirements.section: Methods > Method Definitions > CONNECT
requirements.text: There is no default port; a client MUST send the port number even if the CONNECT request is based on a URI reference that contains an authority component with an elided port (Section 4.1).

requirements.section: Methods > Method Definitions > CONNECT
requirements.text: A server MUST NOT send any Transfer-Encoding or Content-Length header fields in a 2xx (Successful) response to CONNECT.

requirements.section: Methods > Method Definitions > CONNECT
requirements.text: A server MUST reject a CONNECT request that targets an empty or invalid port number, typically by responding with a 400 (Bad Request) status code.

requirements.section: Methods > Method Definitions > CONNECT
requirements.text: A tunnel is closed when a tunnel intermediary detects that either side has closed its connection: the intermediary MUST attempt to send any outstanding data that came from the closed side to the other side, close both connections, and then discard any remaining data left undelivered.

requirements.section: Methods > Method Definitions > CONNECT
requirements.text: Proxies that support CONNECT SHOULD restrict its use to a limited set of known ports or a configurable list of safe request targets.

requirements.section: Methods > Method Definitions > OPTIONS
requirements.text: A client MAY send a Max-Forwards header field in an OPTIONS request to target a specific recipient in the request chain (see Section 7.6.2).

requirements.section: Methods > Method Definitions > OPTIONS
requirements.text: A client that generates an OPTIONS request containing content MUST send a valid Content-Type header field describing the representation media type.

requirements.section: Methods > Method Definitions > OPTIONS
requirements.text: A proxy MUST NOT generate a Max-Forwards header field while forwarding a request unless that request was received with a Max-Forwards field.

requirements.section: Methods > Method Definitions > OPTIONS
requirements.text: A server generating a successful response to OPTIONS SHOULD send any header that might indicate optional features implemented by the server and applicable to the target resource (e.g., Allow), including potential extensions not defined by this specification.

requirements.section: Methods > Method Definitions > TRACE
requirements.text: A client MUST NOT generate fields in a TRACE request containing sensitive data that might be disclosed by the response.

requirements.section: Methods > Method Definitions > TRACE
requirements.text: A client MUST NOT send content in a TRACE request.

requirements.section: Methods > Method Definitions > TRACE
requirements.text: The final recipient of the request SHOULD exclude any request fields that are likely to contain sensitive data when that recipient generates the response content.

requirements.section: Methods > Method Definitions > TRACE
requirements.text: The final recipient of the request SHOULD reflect the message received, excluding some fields described below, back to the client as the content of a 200 (OK) response.
